title: Great reviews are not the same as knowing why people chose you
argument: Reviews show that clients were happy. They do not show what tipped a couple into choosing you, and only that second answer tells you what your ads should say.
audience: Established wedding venues and pros with good reviews who assume testimonials already tell them how couples decide, and who want their ads and messaging to speak to real buying triggers.
tension: Owners with glowing reviews can feel they already know their buyers, yet nobody has asked the newest clients what made them say yes.
take: Reviews show that clients were happy. They do not show what tipped a couple into choosing you, and only that second answer tells you what your ads should say.
mechanism: Whitney draws on what she hears when onboarding full-service clients, separates reviews from decision-factor research, and recommends a short post-signing survey in LeadLock so both the client and WIA see the answers and can feed them into the advertising strategy.
source_assertions: [moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney said that when onboarding full-service clients she often asks whether they have market research, and that the usual response is that they have great reviews.
[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney distinguished reviews from market research, describing research as asking a new client why they signed and what their deciding factors were.

[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney said those answers could be layered back into ad or marketing strategy, and offered to create a market research survey in LeadLock for both of the client's offerings, sent about a week after a client signs.
[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Whitney said both the client and WIA would see the responses, and described the aim as learning buying triggers so the ads can attract more of the right people.
[moment_1fd04cdedc6080e01f4a40d6] Mike said it was a great idea and Marisa said she would do it.
inference: Reviews and decision-factor research answer different questions, and treating one as a substitute for the other leaves a gap in messaging strategy.

title: Why the question of why they chose you and the question of what the musician should know belong in different forms
argument: Learning why someone bought and preparing to serve them are different questions. They are best asked at different moments, in different forms, for different readers.
audience: Wedding businesses with a team of performers or vendors who want to know more about their couples, both to sell better and to deliver a more personal day.
tension: It is tempting to ask everything in one form, but a short, timely buying-decision survey and a thorough wedding-day planning form do different jobs.
take: Learning why someone bought and preparing to serve them are different questions. They are best asked at different moments, in different forms, for different readers.
mechanism: Whitney recommended a short research survey (about five questions, mostly multiple choice, one or two open-ended) sent within days to a week of signing, while the buying decision is fresh. She put it in LeadLock and recommended a separate pre-wedding planning form in the client's CRM that can be shared with the performers.
source_assertions: [moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Marisa said it would help the DJs to know more about the couple, such as a meaningful detail that makes performers feel part of the couple's story.
[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Mike said it would be interesting to learn what attracted buyers, for example the saxophonist or the lighting.
[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Marisa asked whether the questions should go out from LeadLock or be added to a revamped, more comprehensive wedding info form.

[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Whitney said she would treat them as two separate things. She recommended a market research survey sent a couple of days to a week after signing, with about five questions, mostly multiple choice, built in LeadLock.
[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Whitney recommended a separate pre-wedding planning form in the client's CRM for wedding-day needs that could be shared with musicians or the band.

[moment_0ced0a098e016faa7be084e1] Marisa said she could paste the survey link into the existing welcome flow, and Whitney confirmed the survey would be built in LeadLock and could be emailed from anywhere.
inference: Separating the two purposes keeps the research short and well timed, while letting the operational form be as thorough as the team needs.
qualifiers: All of this is a proposal. Completion, welcome-flow placement and resulting insights are not established.
The suggested benefits for musicians and examples of what attracted buyers came from the clients, not from survey findings.

The possible benefit to musicians and the examples of what attracted buyers came from the clients, not from verified survey findings.

title: What attribution can't see: the couple who clicks an ad now and inquires on their own two weeks later
argument: Attribution data tells you what came through the ads. It does not tell you everything the ads influenced, so check that the ads work in isolation and also that the whole business is moving.
audience: Wedding business owners evaluating their ads who either credit only tracked leads or struggle to connect ad reports to overall business growth.
tension: Some bookings, such as planner referrals, arrive with no known source, and some leads say they saw the business on Instagram without anyone knowing whether it was an ad.
take: Attribution data tells you what came through the ads. It does not tell you everything the ads influenced, so check that the ads work in isolation and also that the whole business is moving.
mechanism: Whitney proposed adding sales figures to reports and having Carmen pull the January to April sales history. She also explained the ad-then-organic customer journey and why direct attribution and overall performance give different information.
source_assertions: [moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney said reports would include actual sales, not just booked calls, and said Carmen had found that one Google Ads lead in May turned into a $14,000 booking for the client's higher-priced offering.
[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney said that one May booking covered everything spent on ads that year, and gave a rough ROI of about 7x with "something like that."
[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Mike said the accountant and bookkeeper indicated the business was up about 30% year to date.

[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Whitney said the reports show leads attributed to ads, but that ads can have an impact not visible in attribution data, describing someone who clicks an ad, researches the business, and inquires organically a week or two later.

[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Mike said some bookings are not in LeadLock because planners contact him directly, and he does not know how those clients found the business. Whitney raised that planners may have seen ads.
[moment_685c9db487511394f76b1711] Marisa said callers almost always say they think they saw the business on Instagram, which she assumed must be an ad.
inference: Ad-attributed results and overall business movement answer different questions, and treating either as the whole picture is misleading.
qualifiers: The $14,000 booking is reported in the meeting. There is no independent verification or collected-revenue detail, and the cost basis for the claim that it covers ad spend was not stated.
The 7x figure was an off-the-cuff estimate and should not be used as a result.
The 30% increase was attributed to the accountant and bookkeeper. Its period and calculation were not detailed, and it is not attributed to ads.
Whitney's ad-to-organic journey is a possible explanation, not a demonstration for the untracked planner bookings.
Marisa's Instagram comments were anecdotal and did not establish whether callers saw organic content or an ad.

title: A niche ad campaign with almost no clicks: what to watch before you turn it off
argument: A campaign with little search demand and no clicks isn't costing much. The one to worry about is the one getting clicks without leads.
audience: Wedding business owners running or considering ads for a smaller service, a secondary offer, or a limited local market.
tension: It's uncomfortable to keep an ad running that isn't producing anything, but stopping may mean missing a seasonal window you can't see yet.
take: A campaign with little search demand and no clicks isn't costing much. The one to worry about is the one getting clicks without leads.
mechanism: Carmen explained the low search volume and the broadened keywords, asked when inquiries usually arrive, said click costs are not incurred without clicks, named clicks without leads as the trigger to reconsider, and suggested a visual Meta test. Whitney guessed that back-to-school could bring more traction.
source_assertions: [moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen said the senior-photos campaign had very low search volume, about 10 searches a month on average for her keywords in the local area, and that she broadened the targeting to anything senior-related but still got impressions and no clicks.
[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Bri said senior inquiries are not high volume, probably fewer than 10 a month and fairly stable, and wondered whether the season mattered.
[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen said she did not think it hurt to keep it running, and Bri said she doesn't pay unless people click.

[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen said a spike might come around the start of school in August or September, and that the only problem with keeping a campaign on is getting clicks and no leads, which would be a waste of money.
[moment_573c3e6d0094fc6fa6fd0259] Carmen suggested that if Bri ran Meta, senior photos might do well on Instagram. Whitney guessed there may be more traction with back to school.
inference: The decision is about spending exposure and a plausible seasonal window, not a blanket rule for when to keep or stop a campaign.

title: When inquiries slow down, the first question is whether it's only the ads
argument: Before changing a campaign, find out whether the slowdown is limited to paid ads or shows up everywhere, then look at targeting and the landing experience with the client.
audience: Venue and wedding pro owners who notice a drop in inquiries and aren't sure whether to blame their ads, the season, or something else.
tension: A burst of leads after a change feels like proof, but the same pattern can return, and two changes at once make it hard to know which one mattered.
take: Before changing a campaign, find out whether the slowdown is limited to paid ads or shows up everywhere, then look at targeting and the landing experience with the client.
mechanism: Fallon asked whether the slowdown also appeared organically and verified it in LeadLock. She applied the client's more specific locations to Google targeting and identified the ads or the page as the remaining suspects, reasoning that leads were not failing to book tours. She also planned to look further back at historical trends.

title: Judging a campaign change fairly: line up the dates and ask what each conversion actually is
argument: Before saying a change worked, compare matching periods, check what a conversion counts, and expect daily results to move in spikes.
audience: Owners or small teams making campaign changes and trying to read the numbers afterward.
tension: The numbers looked like improvement, yet the date range changed the answer and a booked appointment is not always a new, qualified client.
take: Before saying a change worked, compare matching periods, check what a conversion counts, and expect daily results to move in spikes.
mechanism: Carmen found the change date in the account's change history, compared the periods before and after, corrected the date range when her figures differed, discussed the daily spikes, and shared her view that the campaign was trending in a better direction.
source_assertions: [moment_c802d7cb180271683939f39f] Carmen used the account's change history to find that the campaign was changed back to Maximize Clicks on June 4.

[moment_c802d7cb180271683939f39f] Carmen read the earlier period (May 19 to June 4) as a cost per conversion of $64 and four booked appointments, then looked at June 4 to date at a cost per conversion of about $57.

[moment_c802d7cb180271683939f39f] Carmen noticed her morning figure of $45 differed because she had been viewing a different date range (June 1 to 16), and corrected the booked-appointment count to three.
[moment_c802d7cb180271683939f39f] Jillian said conversions are people who made an appointment, some were repeats, two or three were new, and one cancelled because she missed the location.

[moment_c802d7cb180271683939f39f] Carmen said daily cost per booked appointment came in spikes, for example about $15, $7 and $17 on different days, and said she thought the campaign was trending in the right direction though she wished the change were more dramatic.
[moment_c802d7cb180271683939f39f] Jillian said she thought it was a good choice to switch it back and noted that appointment requests had always arrived in bursts.
